feed.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Wallet label synchronization (BIP-329 records over encrypted stores)

entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Wallet label synchronization (BIP-329 records over encrypted stores)
entry.summary: The discussion revolves around the challenges and proposed solutions for synchronizing wallet labels across multiple wallets using the same descriptor, as highlighted by the limitations of BIP-329. A new approach is suggested to enhance the synchronization process through a shared, untrusted store that utilizes deterministic discovery, encrypted envelopes with merge semantics, and transport agnosticism. The deterministic discovery would allow wallets to derive a storage location and encryption keys from the wallet descriptor, enabling different wallets (such as a coordinator and a watch-only wallet) to access the same data seamlessly without any configuration or use of private keys. This method ensures that both types of wallets function efficiently without compromising privacy or security. The proposal includes storing records in an AEAD-encrypted envelope which carries not only the data but also an author timestamp and provisions for handling deletions via tombstones, as BIP-329 does not inherently support record deletion. The merging process would be governed by a last-write-wins rule based on the timestamps within the ciphertext, ensuring integrity and freshness of the data while preventing potential conflicts from concurrent edits. To address issues of data volume and pruning by stores, periodic full snapshots are proposed, allowing for restoration in fresh wallets and accommodating stores that may not maintain a complete history. Furthermore, the system's design is meant to be transport agnostic, suggesting that while Nostr relays could serve as the reference transport method due to their suitability for handling snapshot addresses and delta events, other methods like HTTPS stores or synced folders might also be adequate. This flexibility ensures that the system can adapt to various infrastructural constraints while maintaining security and privacy, as the store would not learn about the content and cannot forge records. The email also delves into considerations for key derivation modes and identity models, highlighting a choice between a zero-interaction restore using descriptor-derived keys and a more secure but less convenient model involving an independent random sync secret. Additionally, it raises questions about whether to maintain a simple shared key system or to involve more complex setups requiring manual approvals per device. Craig, another contributor, emphasizes the need to consider these proposals within a broader context of inter-wallet communication standards, suggesting that wallet developers would benefit from a unified approach rather than bespoke solutions for different data formats. He expresses reservations about using Nostr as the primary transport, suggesting that privacy should be prioritized over other factors like censorship resistance. His ongoing work on a BIP for canonical output descriptors could also influence the standardization process, stressing the importance of considering scope and privacy implications in designing these systems. For further insights and detailed discussions on this topic, Craig refers to a previous contribution which can be explored in depth [here](https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev/c/GTIO4xDX5MU/m/-MoPJhiTAwAJ).
